Bennarius
I would only recommend this game to hardcore fans. Exploring the world is fun, but the pacing gets completely ruined when you’re stuck on a boss for several hours. Sometimes you spend five minutes getting back to the boss just to die in five seconds, repeating the process until you’ve memorized every attack through muscle memory. That doesn’t feel like skill to me, just mindless repetition. (I completely finished the first Hollow Knight without any major difficulties.) There’s also no real fast travel, some checkpoints feel unfairly placed, and there’s no “normal” difficulty option. Overall, the game feels extremely disrespectful of the player’s time. I played about 70% of it before quitting, and I haven’t touched it since.

martian0_0muse
Silksong is hard, but not in a rewarding way. The game relies heavily on what feels like cheap, artificial difficulty design: inflated damage, cluttered encounters, and boss mechanics that prioritize ambiguity over clarity. Fights like the second Lace encounter highlight the core issue. When attacks share similar tells but require different responses, success stops being about learning and starts feeling like guessing. That breaks the sense of fairness and makes improvement inconsistent. The pacing makes things worse. Difficulty spikes are stacked back to back with little breathing room. The game introduces optional upgrades without clearly signaling whether you should pursue them. This creates confusion about progression and leaves players feeling underpowered or misdirected. The economy adds another layer of frustration. The introduction of multiple currencies, especially tools requiring a separate and limited resource, feels poorly balanced. Early on, resources are scarce when you need them most, making retries and experimentation punishing. Later, they become abundant when they matter less. This adds friction without adding meaningful challenge. Even retrying boss fights becomes tedious. Deaths often require long backtracking through respawned enemies just to get another attempt. Failure becomes a chore instead of a learning opportunity. Rather than encouraging mastery, the game stacks frustration on top of already punishing encounters. Silksong does not build on what made Hollow Knight great: clear telegraphs, learnable fights, and satisfying challenge. Instead, it increases difficulty without adding depth. The result is a harder game that is far more frustrating than its predecessor. Challenging games can be fun. This one too often forgets that.

OniMode
What would otherwise be a 9/10 game is reduced to 4 over one specific, awful design choice. It's entirely expected that boss fights are about learning and multiple attempts. A good game would allow some space in between each attempt, but really only enough time to catch a breath. Silksong decided to have minute long runbacks that offer little more than a repetitive slog between each attempt. It's not nearly as much of a skill issue as it is a time issue. As an adult with limited time for gaming, I want to spend that time enjoying myself. I've played and beaten a lot of the games people would consider difficult, so 'git gud' doesn't apply here. Would you choose to go to the longest line to buy groceries? Would you choose to sit in traffic? Would you read a book that had pauses in between page turns? Of course not. I would strongly advise either holding off on purchasing this game until it's addressed, which I suspect it won't be, or purchasing this on PC and using a mod.

DieterU
Silksong is another incredible journey into a kingdom not unlike Hallownest, but this time through the eyes of Hornet. Compared to her nearly hollow counterpart, The Knight, Hornet is much more of a fleshed out "character," as she speaks and has a lot of personality and motivation of her own. Both approaches work well in their respective games, as The Knight's demeanor seems beffitting of a nearly dead kingdom, whereas Pharloom is a lot more lively and filled with a bunch of personalities. Another notable difference is the gender of our protagonists: Hornet is a woman. And this game is in many ways, very much about women. Most of the main cast is consisted of women, and we examine a few mother-daughter relationships, and we see through Hornet's eyes that the world is not a very friendly place to women! She is, of course, a much tougher bug than most, but there are multiple instances where gross man bugs who seriously underestimate her abilities try to harass her, and it does NOT go well for **** world Hornet is transported to is gorgeous, almost beyond belief. The drawings are so detailed and lush; exploring Pharloom is seriously magical at times. I think my favorite area was Shellwood, where bugs have evolved alongside plants, and each took on some characteristics of the **** of the biggest questions that a lot of us had going in to this game was how the gameplay and difficulty was going to compare to the first game. Hornet's arsenal of abilities and tools was a significant upgrade from The Knight's. Her incredibly agile movement feels so good to control, and all of the tools and crests she acquires give a great variety of play styles. The difficulty is the big topic that nobody seems to be able to come to a consensus on. My personal experience was that Act 1 was incredibly difficult, but Acts 2 and 3 were much easier, and at times a little too easy. I think the ease of the latter thirds of the game was largely in part to the Wanderer's crest, which I didn't start using until fairly late. I didn't mind the high difficulty of the early game because I personally just really enjoy bashing my head against a boss over and over again until I can learn their moveset to a really precise degree. And I felt that that was missing from some of the late game bosses. I had a lot of fun fighting Karmelita, who is probably my favorite boss of the game, but I beat her on my fifth try when I was expecting to be stuck on her for hours on end. For my first three attempts against her I was using the Reaper Crest, but realized that it was going to be way too hard, so I switched to Wanderer and killed her two attempts later. So I think the bosses are really excellent and the difficulty is mostly good, but the Wanderer Crest just needs some slight reworking. I don't want to be forced to nerf myself to have a higher enjoyment of the game, because I just feel stupid if I'm stuck on a boss for a long time and the tools to defeat her are right at my fingertips. Nonetheless, the combat always felt incredibly fun and was a big step up from the first game in almost every way. Excellent game.

Mclintoc
I finished my first play-through (including Act 3). The first Hollow Knight is my favorite game of all time. Thus, I had big expectations for Silksong. I can say it is everything I hoped it would be, having all the elements of the first game in a more expansive and varied world: Precise gameplay and design, beautiful art and music, a fascinating and immersive story. It is certainly harder than Hollow Knight, but this is what I wanted and the game is never unfair. (More on this at the end) Given the long development process, there were more bugs than I expected, but I imagine these will get worked out over time. My only real complaint is the crest system. I did not like it at first. I have since warmed to it a little as it makes the game more customizable and gameplay more strategic, but overall I have just found it to be annoying. An important part of a Metroidvania is to move from powerless to powerful. The crest system is a lateral rather than upward movement and a few crests have terrible downward pogos--an essential skill for the game. Nevertheless, like I said, this game is everything I hoped it would be and I will be playing it for many, many more hours to come. Many have complained about the difficulty. I completed the original Hollow Knight with 112% in Steel Soul mode and completed Pantheon of Hallownest. Thus, I was well prepared for the difficulty and am so glad Team Cherry made the game harder. There is real consequence to decisions and you can see yourself getting better and better with each boss fight. I love the sense of accomplishment the game gives, and Team Cherry should be praised for this. Yes, it's not for everyone, but, as I said, the game is never unfair, and it gives someone who loved Hollow Knight just what they wanted. Git Gud!

SophieHix
Silksong is the first Hollow Knight game I have played and it will be the only. I have played video games for all of my life and often play on hard modes, but Hollow Knight has no difficulty settings yet is unbelievable impossible to play. I spend more hours watching how-to videos on youtube than actually playing the game, and each arena/miniboss/boss takes around 4 hours or 50-100 attempts each. But the difficulty isn’t even the worst thing. Every battle is far from a save point meaning you have to monotonously trek/fight past multiple enemies and jumps on the way back to the arena, and if you die before reaching your previous death location you lose all the currency you have worked hours for. So each time you die, you lose any hope of gaining better weapons or exploring alternative areas due to having no currency to achieve these plans. The game style and art is beautiful, but the difficulty and mechanics make it the only game I’ve ever felt physically angry while playing. You are better off having never started.

My vote for GOTY will definitely for Silksong. First time ever, I bought a digital game at full price. The fact that they make it affordable just made me want to fully support them. Besides that, the game runs flawlessly on Switch. No lag or performance issue, visual is the same like the original Hollow Knight which great, vibrant and lively. Now to the gameplay itself. On the other side there are more tools so I see no reason for it being too difficult or punishing. For context, I finish the game and reach true ending, not completing it yet. Besides that, we also get 7 different play style which nuts. Some are lackluster but the fact they provide us with 7 different approach in combat is amazing. Plus, we can synergies each tool to specific play style so we can play around to find combo that suit our style. I'm 60+ hours in and there's still so much more to discover. With that amount of content, I feel the value of the game is way much more than what its priced. Well recommended and must buy for metroidvania fans. ultrasoft
I've been on a rollercoaster with Silksong. From highly dissapointed, to love, and then dissapointment again. I have now settled on this; I love it mechanically but it doesn't quite do it for me on many other levels. In this way it feels like my relationship with Dark Souls 3 in comparison to Dark Souls 1, mechanically much improved, stuffed with cool toys and details, but a lesser game in some ways, lacking a the vibe and soul that made me lovr the earlier game. I wrote my first review of Silksong in a bit of a temper. I thought this is too hard, they went bananas with the difficulty. I struggled with many bosses. I put the game down for a while at the end of act 1. Picked it back up a few days later and replayed from the start. I found a few more tools, got more practice, and enjoyed it more, eventually cracked into act 2. I was killing bosses in less attempts, getting through the game way faster. I've started about 4 or 5 games now and I am contemplating the speedrunning challenge. All my earlier complaints about difficulty, pacing, or the economy have melted as I have practiced and (thankfully) improved, and my knowlege of the game has grown. It's certainly a challenge though and if you aren't great at action video gaming like me it might take you a lot of practice, time, and patience to get competent at, and through Silksong. I am left feeling a little dissapointed that there isn't quite the same magic as I felt there was in HK, and there isn't anything really that innovative. Most of Silksongs tricks have been done before, most of the surprises feel like stuff we've seen before in Dark Souls or Bloodborne. Which are fun references but I am disappointed that the game lacks any really interesting twists of its own. In short, it's good, well priced, challenging, feels great in the hands once you get competent enough to enjoy it, unfortunately not quite as stellar as it's predecessor or I want it to be. I doubt DLC can push it up there but hey, we will have to see.

It’s hard to create a game where you can do just about anything, go almost anywhere at any time. And it’s even harder to not only make it brutally difficult, but annoyingly addictive. (In other words: the game is very hard, but very fun.)Team Cherry did it. They crafted a near perfect experience filled to the brim with fun challenges, endless collectibles and secrets, mysterious lore, and tough but fair combat. I understand that not all gamers can fully enjoy an experience such as this, what with the Last Judge shaped elephant in the room, but even those who did not see this game or it’s predecessor through to the end must admit the achievement we were alive to witness that is this game. Call me a “glazer” all you want, but this game deserves all the praise it gets, and more. And for $19.99! Mario Kart WHO?! My conclusion: buy this game. You have nothing to lose. Torby
30 years after the release of Super Metroid and almost 15 years after the release of Dark Souls, Hollow Knight: Silksong creates a new gold standard by fusing together and mastering the best parts of both games and their genres. 2017's Hollow Knight already did this to some extent, but personally I found it to be too bleak and too unpolished in its level design. I now appreciate it more however, as it prepared me for this adventure. Hollow Knight: Silksong sports breathtaking visuals and an immersive soundtrack that takes you away into Pharloom, an expansive world that never fails to surprise you without feeling too overwhelming. Every area has distinct environments and enemies, with intuitive level design and paths that you quickly get used to traversing. Inaccessible areas are clearly marked as such, with clues that will have you returning later to explore more. These are basics of a Metroidvania, but it is seldom done this precisely and to this scale. Even after putting 50 hours into the game, I still found new paths that interconnected areas in unexpected ways and gave me that "aha!" moment. Just as the creators promised, this is a handcrafted and gorgeous world to explore, from the depths of the Deep Docks to the High Halls of the Citadel. The story borrows heavily from Fromsoftware's style, with a bleak, overarching story that you can affect the outcome of, and with its memorable characters that you follow and interact with throughout the world. But as opposed to Dark Souls, it's much easier to follow and track. The new quest system is surprisingly fleshed out, and pairs perfectly with the backtracking that is normally found in the genre. Suddenly I found myself donating to charity, participating in a race, or even buying a house! And imagine my relief when I found out that you can 100% the game on your first save file, even after doing the "standard" ending and "missing" things in one of the game's acts. Whereas for instance Elden Ring forces you to replay the entire game's 30+ hour campaign to see a different ending. Hollow Knight: Silksong is tough, but fair. It gives the player all the necessary tools to succeed and more, but also trusts them with the responsibility of finding them and learning how they work. It follows in the footsteps of its predecessors and rewards experimentation and exploration to a high degree. The new crest system allows players to alter Hornet's moveset, and the new tools gives you a plethora of ways to fight. The movement and gameplay itself is extremely versatile and responsive, more so than in Hollow Knight. Fighting enemies and bosses has never been more fun! So, what are the negatives? The challenge is significant, and may seem daunting. And since the game goes for a "show don't tell" style, players might find themselves stuck at different points, not knowing how to beat a boss or progress a specific quest. While I do think the game could use an accessibility option, I also respect the creator vision and their decision to keep the game as is. No game is for everyone, and that is especially true here. But *if* you want to experience Silksong, don't be discouraged it's reputation. The required boss fights for the standard ending are completely surmountable, and looking up how to get a few useful items will quickly get you ahead if you're struggling. And even if you keep dying, the game rarely feels unfair or frustrating. That is not to say there aren't critique worthy parts of the game. The in-game economy is rough at times, and some boss fights or "runbacks" are more difficult than they need to be. It's hard to pin these down as truly negative aspects, as they elevate other parts of the experience. The limited ammo for tools are there because they do make boss fights significantly easier. And the frustrating areas such as "Bilewater", tests the player's skills and offers an optional challenge to who dares take it. That being said, yes, the game pushes the bar too far at times, undoubtedly frustrating many players. If that's the case, why is it deserving of a perfect score? To me, personally, it's the extreme amount of polish, value for its price tag, and the feeling of "extra" that I'm left with after playing it. You could finish this as a standard Metroidvania experience in 20 hours and be left satisfied. But as opposed to most other Metroidvania experiences out there, this game just keeps on giving and giving if you put more time into it. And finally, I have to talk about the boss fights. There is an huge gauntlet of challenging bosses feel amazing to master. Their variety, scale and polish is nothing short of perfection. Even as a huge Fromsoftware fan, I have to say that I've never had this much fun with bosses in a game before. Hollow Knight: Silksong offers an amazing amount of value for its price tag, and expands upon and develops the Metroidvania genre to new heights. Honestly, I can't praise it enough. Thanks for reading.

Warum Silksong aus meiner Perspektive kein gutes Spiel ist... Hollow Knight: Silksong ist ein wunderschönes Spiel. Eine atemberaubende bezaubernde Welt mit vielen Verstecken und Geheimnissen. Viele liebevoll gestaltete Gebiete. Von Lavewelten und alten Schmieden zu Städten einer sterbenden Hochkultur. Verträumte Gärten, mythische Wälder, dunkle Abgründe und göttliche Welten. Es ist alles dabei. Eine kluge, in sich schlüssige Welt. Das ist den Entwicklern sehr gut gelungen. Hornet als Protagonistin ist auch faszinierend. Dieses Mal eine Heldin, die redet, Dialoge führt und die Welt auf eine neue Art kennenlernt. Die Geschichte, die man mehr und mehr entschlüsselt je tiefer wir in die Welt eindringen, verzaubert und berührt. Eine Geschichte mit Humor, Drama und jede Menge Wirren. Dies ist auch sehr gut gelungen. Das Gameplay, Platforming und Kämpfen macht auch sehr viel Spass. Das Rumprobieren mit verschiedenen Werkzeugen und Fähigkeiten, die man entdeckt sind schon cool. Und es gibt jede Menge Möglichkeit kreativ zu sein und sich auszuleben. Auch die Gegner und Bosse sind sehr verschieden und überraschen immer wieder. Die Bewegungen sind flüssig. Ich habe nie irgendwelche Lacks oder Fehler festgestellt. Auch der Preis der Entwickler ist sehr entgegenkommend und eine Liebeserklärung an die Community. Trotzt allem ist Silksong für mich kein gutes Spiel. Die Wertung wäre notmalerweise bei 9 bis 10. Hinzukommt aber der Schwierigkeitsgrad. Ich bin Schwierigkeit gewöhnt. Von Elden Ring zu Dark Souls habe ich jedes Soulslike durch. Jede Herausforderung gemeistert. Es war hart und schwierig. Aber das Lernen und das Meistern hat immer letzten Endes Spass gemacht. Aber Silksong hat mir die Freude genommen. Bosse fordernd zu gestalten ist immer gut. Zu lernen und sich zu verbessern ist das ultimative Gamingerlebnis. Zumindest für mich. Dieses Gefühl hatte ich hier nicht. Es gab Kämpfe, die gut waren. Aber dann gab es einfach Passagen, wo erstmal eine schwierigr Platforming Abschnitt kommt und dann der Boss. Wenn der Boss einen besiegt. Muss das Platforming nochmal gemacht werden. Und das ist mega frustrierend. Klar lernt man das irgendwann. Klar meistert man das Plattforming. Klar legt man irgendwann den Boss. Aber es fühlt sich dann nur noch wie eine monotone stupide Wiederholung an. Vor allem frustrierend ist es wenn man einen so mega schwierigen Abschnitt schafft und es dann nicht mal eine Belohnung gibt. Stattdessen kommt der Absturz in ein schwierigeres Gebiet. Indem man zusätzlich gefangen ist und auch noch Safepoint immer wieder kaufen muss. Das sind Designentscheidungen die mich insgesamt frustriert haben. Auch wichtige Items hinter Quests zu verstecken, die langwierig und teilweise zufallsabhängig sind, finde ich genauso unverständlich. Genauso Safepoints nach einer schwierigen Platforming Passage mit Fallen zu bestücken, finde ich auch daneben. Das ist einfach nicht witzig. Irgendwann hat sich dieses Spiel dann nur noch wie eine langweillige, monotone Wiederholung ohne richtige Erfolgserlebnisse angefühlt. Aufgrunddessen gibt es auch ein massive Abwertung meinerseits. Auf 7 Punkte insgesamt.
